+# Windows Server 2028 Preview: New features | Microsoft Learn
+
+Windows Server 2028 Preview introduces new capabilities across identity, management, automation, security, recovery, storage, and virtualization. Administrators and technical decision-makers can evaluate these capabilities before release to identify features that merit testing and deployment planning.
+
+This article summarizes the features available for evaluation and identifies the first Windows Server Insider Preview build in which each feature appeared. To begin evaluating the features, see [Get started with Windows Server Insider Preview](get-started-with-windows-server-insiders-preview).
+
+Important
+
+Windows Server 2028 is currently in PREVIEW. This information relates to a prerelease product that may be substantially modified before it's released. Microsoft makes no warranties, expressed or implied, with respect to the information provided here.
+
+For build-specific limitations and workarounds, see the known issues in the announcements for [Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706](https://aka.ms/serverinsiders), [Windows Server Insider Preview build 29683](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/discussions/windowsserverinsiders/announcing-windows-server-vnext-preview-build-29683/4563923), and [Windows Server Insider Preview build 29651](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/discussions/windowsserverinsiders/announcing-windows-server-vnext-preview-build-29651/4549702).
+
+## PowerShell 7
+
+**Insider Preview build:**[Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706](https://aka.ms/serverinsiders) (November 17, 2026)
+
+Windows Server 2028 Preview includes PowerShell 7, providing an upgrade path from Windows PowerShell 5.1. Windows PowerShell 5.1 remains available side by side, so existing automation can continue to use it without a forced migration. For more information, see [What's new in PowerShell](/en-us/powershell/scripting/whats-new/overview).
+
+## SMB Policy Controller
+
+**Insider Preview build:**[Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706](https://aka.ms/serverinsiders) (November 17, 2026)
+
+SMB Policy Controller in Windows Server 2028 Preview helps administrators reduce manual configuration and keep Server Message Block (SMB) file-share settings aligned with workload needs. Instead of configuring each managed setting individually, use PowerShell to define the intended use of an existing share, such as departmental file storage or application data, and select a security- or performance-oriented profile. You can manage share-specific and server-wide settings separately. The controller applies the managed configuration and reconciles drift to maintain the intended settings over time.
+
+## Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft Intune management for Windows Server
+
+**Insider Preview build:**[Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706](https://aka.ms/serverinsiders) (November 17, 2026)
+
+Windows Server 2028 Preview can join Microsoft Entra ID through **Settings** > **Accounts** > **Access work or school**, using the same Settings flow as Windows 11. Administrators can then sign in to Windows Server with Microsoft Entra accounts.
+
+Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft Intune can work alongside Azure Arc on the same server within the scope supported by this preview. Microsoft Intune provides endpoint-management workflows, while Azure Arc provides infrastructure management, monitoring, and governance. In Microsoft Intune environments that opt in to server enrollment, servers that meet the [Windows Server management in Intune requirements](https://aka.ms/IntuneServerGuide) automatically enroll in Microsoft Intune so endpoint administrators can manage them alongside Windows clients. Microsoft Intune server enrollment is off by default and intended for nonproduction preview evaluation.
+
+Identity capabilities include:
+
+- Join Microsoft Entra ID through **Settings** without requiring Active Directory Domain Services for the join.
+- Sign in to Windows Server with Microsoft Entra accounts.
+- Use device compliance as a signal for Microsoft Entra Conditional Access.
+- Use Microsoft Entra accounts with administrative privileges to access supported Windows Server capabilities.
+
+Management capabilities include:
+
+- Automatically enroll Microsoft Entra joined servers in Microsoft Intune, or use Group Policy to enroll Microsoft Entra hybrid joined servers.
+- View operating system and application inventory.
+- Apply security baselines and device configuration policies supported in the Microsoft Intune server management preview through configuration service providers (CSPs).
+- Deploy supported Win32 apps.
+- Manage updates by using Windows Update for Business and Windows Autopatch settings supported in the Microsoft Intune server management preview.
+
+Existing Microsoft Intune roles, scope tags, groups, and assignment filters control access and policy targeting. If Group Policy, Configuration Manager, Azure Arc, Microsoft Intune, or another tool manages the server, avoid enforcing conflicting settings.
+
+For more information, see [Get started with Windows Server management in Intune](https://aka.ms/IntuneServerGuide).
+
+To share feedback about the preview, submit the [Intune Server Management preview feedback form](https://forms.cloud.microsoft/r/ax1xF5ccUC) or visit the [Windows Server Insiders community](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/category/windows-server/discussions/windowsserverinsiders). For preview issues, use these feedback channels instead of contacting Microsoft support.
+
+## Secure by default for Server Core
+
+**Insider Preview build:**[Windows Server Insider Preview build 29683](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/discussions/windowsserverinsiders/announcing-windows-server-vnext-preview-build-29683/4563923) (October 12, 2026)
+
+Windows Server 2028 Preview includes secure-by-default configuration settings for Server Core. New installations start with stronger security protections. This change reduces the need to harden servers after deployment. These defaults help protect servers against common attacks, including credential theft, lateral movement, and protocol downgrade attacks, from the first boot.
+
+The hardened defaults fall into seven layers:
+
+- Network exposure
+- Identity and authentication
+- Privilege and administrative access
+- Remote access and management
+- Cryptography
+- Operating system platform and code integrity
+- Observability
+
+This preview applies hardened defaults to new installations only. For more information, see [Secure by default for Windows Server](https://aka.ms/WSHardened).
+
+## Trusted Launch for Generation 2 virtual machines
+
+**Insider Preview build:**[Windows Server Insider Preview build 29621](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/discussions/windowsserverinsiders/announcing-windows-server-vnext-preview-build-29621/4536572) (July 13, 2026)
+
+Trusted Launch in Windows Server 2028 Preview helps administrators protect Generation 2 Hyper-V workloads from boot-level and firmware attacks that can compromise a virtual machine (VM) before operating-system defenses start. It uses Secure Boot, a virtual Trusted Platform Module (vTPM), and encrypted guest state. This preview doesn't support:
+
+- Moving a Trusted Launch VM to another server.
+- Using Trusted Launch VMs with failover clusters.
+- Using Trusted Launch VMs with Hyper-V Replica.
+- Verifying boot integrity.
+
+For more information, see [Trusted Launch for virtual machines for Windows Server Insiders](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/windowsservernewsandbestpractices/announcing-trusted-launch-for-virtual-machines-for-windows-server-insiders/4537082).
+
+## Quick Machine Recovery
+
+**Insider Preview build:**[Windows Server Insider Preview build 29574](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/discussions/windowsserverinsiders/announcing-windows-server-vnext-preview-build-29574/4515178) (April 27, 2026)
+
+Quick Machine Recovery helps restore servers that can't start after a critical error, reducing the need for manual recovery. Quick Machine Recovery first appeared in Windows Server 2028 Preview in build 29574. It's also available for Windows Server 2025 beginning with the October 2026 security update. After repeated boot failures, the server enters a network-connected Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE), checks Windows Update for a Microsoft-published remediation, applies it, and restarts. Administrators can control whether this best-effort process runs automatically and set retry intervals and a total wait time. Recovery succeeds only if Microsoft has published an applicable remediation. For more information, see [Quick Machine Recovery](/en-us/windows/configuration/quick-machine-recovery/) and [configure Quick Machine Recovery by using Group Policy](/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/group-policy/configure-quick-machine-recovery-via-group-policy).
+
+## NVMe over Fabrics
+
+**Insider Preview build:**[Windows Server Insider Preview build 29550](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/discussions/windowsserverinsiders/announcing-windows-server-vnext-preview-build-29550/4501665) (March 12, 2026)
+
+The built-in Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) over Fabrics (NVMe-oF) initiator in Windows Server 2028 Preview lets you access remote NVMe storage as Windows disks. Use NVMe over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) on standard Ethernet for broader infrastructure compatibility, or use NVMe over RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) on supported networks for lower latency and higher throughput. You can use this preview only from the command line. It doesn't support multipathing and provides limited recovery in some network failure scenarios. For more information, see [Introducing the Windows NVMe-oF Initiator Preview](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/windowsservernewsandbestpractices/introducing-the-windows-nvme-of-initiator-preview-in-windows-server-insiders-bui/4501344).
+
+## ReFS Boot
+
+**Insider Preview build:**[Windows Server Insider Preview build 29531](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/discussions/windowsserverinsiders/announcing-windows-server-vnext-preview-build-29531/4494655) (February 12, 2026)
+
+ReFS Boot is an optional feature that lets Windows Server 2028 Preview start from a Resilient File System (ReFS)-formatted boot volume. ReFS Boot provides ReFS resilience, performance, and scale for operating system storage. For resilience, ReFS uses metadata checksums, optional integrity streams, and online scrubbing to detect corruption and keep the boot volume online without an offline `chkdsk`. For performance, ReFS speeds up storage-intensive operations such as copying large files and managing virtual machine disks. For scale, ReFS supports volumes and files up to 35 petabytes (PB).
+
+ReFS Boot requires Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) firmware, doesn't support Generation 1 VMs, and creates a Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) partition of at least 2 GB. If the WinRE partition lacks space for a WinRE update, Windows might disable WinRE. If you delete the WinRE partition and extend the ReFS boot volume into that space, restoring WinRE requires a clean installation of Windows Server. For more information, see [ReFS Boot for Windows Server Insiders](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/windowsservernewsandbestpractices/announcing-refs-boot-for-windows-server-insiders/4496592) and [Resilient File System overview](../storage/refs/refs-overview).

+# Configure SMB Policy Controller (preview) | Microsoft Learn
+
+SMB Policy Controller (preview) stores the Server Message Block (SMB) settings you want for a device or an existing file share and corrects managed settings when they drift. Use it when you need server-wide and share-level configuration to stay aligned with a defined security or performance outcome.
+
+In this article, you use Windows PowerShell to manage server-wide and share-level SMB intents through their lifecycle while verifying that the effective configuration matches your intended outcome.
+
+Important
+
+SMB Policy Controller is currently in PREVIEW. This information relates to a prerelease product that may be substantially modified before it's released. Microsoft makes no warranties, expressed or implied, with respect to the information provided here.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- Windows Server Insider Preview build 29707 or later.
+- An elevated Windows PowerShell session on the device. For instructions, see [Start Windows PowerShell with administrative privileges](/en-us/powershell/scripting/windows-powershell/starting-windows-powershell#run-with-administrative-privileges).
+- Administrative access to the affected device. A server intent manages the local SMB server configuration, SMB client configuration, managed SMB registry settings, and alternative-port configuration.
+- An existing SMB share for the share-intent procedures. SMB Policy Controller (preview) doesn't create the share, its folder, or its permissions.
+- Representative clients and user identities for access testing.
+- A change plan that identifies affected servers, shares, clients, and other configuration tools that can change the same SMB settings.
+- A record of the effective SMB settings before you create an intent. Use this record when you verify that removal returned the managed settings to their pre-intent values.
+
+## Install SMB Policy Controller (preview)
+
+On a device that runs Windows Server Insider Preview build 29707 or later, install the SMB Policy Controller (preview) Feature on Demand and verify that it's ready before you configure an intent.
+
+1. Open Windows PowerShell as an administrator.
+2. Enable the SMB Policy Controller Feature on Demand (`PolicyController`) by calling `dism.exe` directly.
+
+    ```powershell
+    dism.exe /Online /Enable-Feature /FeatureName:PolicyController
+    ```
+
+    Use `dism.exe` directly because the DISM PowerShell cmdlets don't enable the SMB Policy Controller Feature on Demand from PowerShell 7.
+3. If DISM requests a restart, restart the device.
+4. If you restarted the device, reopen Windows PowerShell as an administrator.
+5. Verify the module, its commands, and the service.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Import-Module PolicyController -ErrorAction Stop
+    Get-Command -Module PolicyController
+    Get-Service -Name PolicyController
+    ```
+
+    Confirm that the module imports, the command list displays the module's commands, and the `PolicyController` service status is `Running`. If installation verification fails, don't continue to intent configuration.
+
+## Choose an intent scope
+
+Choose a server-wide intent to manage host-wide SMB server, SMB client, managed SMB registry settings, and alternative-port configuration. Choose a share-level intent to manage one named, existing SMB share. The scopes are separate. When both intents exist, verify their combined effective settings.
+
+For details about scope interactions and other tools that manage the same settings, see [Server and share intent](smb-policy-controller#server-and-share-intent).
+
+## Choose a profile and workload selector
+
+Choose the **Security** profile when strengthening SMB protection is the priority. Choose the **Performance** profile when workload performance is the priority and you accept its security and availability tradeoffs. For a share intent, also choose the **User data** workload selector for shares that people and teams use interactively or the **Application data** workload selector for shares that applications use for data. Make these choices before you create the intent. For profile effects, tradeoffs, and workload selector guidance, see [SMB Policy Controller (preview) profiles and workload selectors](smb-policy-controller#profiles-and-workload-selectors). For override behavior and limitations, see [SMB Policy Controller profile-derived overrides](smb-policy-controller#profile-derived-overrides).
+
+For a new intent, use an override object when a supported setting must differ from its profile value. For an existing intent, retrieve the current intent, edit only the required properties, and submit the edited object with `Set-Intent -Override`. This pattern retains settings that you don't intend to change.
+
+## Configure an intent
+
+Select the tab for the intent scope that you want to configure.
+
+# [Server-wide intent](#tab/server-wide-intent)
+A server-wide intent manages host-wide SMB server, SMB client, managed SMB registry settings, and alternative-port configuration. Apply it together with one or more share intents when you need both scopes. To configure a server-wide intent, use the following steps.
+
+1. Check for an existing server-wide intent.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Intent -System
+    ```
+
+    If an intent exists, don't add another one. Use the update procedure instead. If the command reports a read or persistence error, resolve the error before continuing.
+2. Review the current effective SMB configuration and confirm that you chose the **Security** profile when SMB protection is the priority or the **Performance** profile when workload performance is the priority and you accept its security and availability tradeoffs. For detailed guidance, see [SMB Policy Controller (preview) profiles and workload selectors](smb-policy-controller#profiles-and-workload-selectors).
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-SmbServerConfiguration
+    Get-SmbClientConfiguration
+    ```
+3. Create the server-wide Security intent.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Add-Intent -Security
+    ```
+
+    To create a Performance intent instead, use `Add-Intent -Performance`. Don't run both commands.
+
+    When `Add-Intent` completes, SMB Policy Controller (preview) stores the desired intent and started an application attempt. To confirm the effective settings and client access, verify the intent.
+4. Immediately complete the verification procedure.
+
+# [Share-level intent](#tab/share-level-intent)
+A share intent manages one named existing share. It doesn't create the share. Server and share scopes are separate, so verify their combined effective settings when both intents exist. Before you create the intent, choose the **Security** profile when SMB protection is the priority or the **Performance** profile when workload performance is the priority and you accept its tradeoffs. Also choose the **User data** workload selector for interactive shares or the **Application data** workload selector for application data. For details, see [SMB Policy Controller (preview) profiles and workload selectors](smb-policy-controller#profiles-and-workload-selectors). Specify both choices so that the share intent doesn't depend on a server-wide default. To configure a share-level intent, use the following steps.
+
+1. Confirm the share name, path, and scope.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-SmbShare -Name 'Documents' -ErrorAction Stop |
+        Format-List Name, ScopeName, Path, Description, FolderEnumerationMode,
+            CachingMode, LeasingMode, CaTimeout, CompressData, ConcurrentUserLimit,
+            ContinuouslyAvailable, DirectoryHandleLeasing, DisableClientMetadataCaching,
+            EncryptData, IsolatedTransport
+    ```
+
+    Replace `Documents` with the exact share name. The documented intent cmdlets accept `ShareName` but don't provide a scope or path selector. If duplicate share names exist in different scopes, don't use the share-intent procedures in this article because they can't target one of those shares unambiguously.
+2. Check for an existing intent for the share.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Intent -ShareName 'Documents'
+    ```
+
+    If an intent exists, use the update procedure instead. Resolve any read or persistence error before treating the result as no intent.
+3. Create a Security-profile intent for a user-data share.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Add-Intent -Security -ShareName 'Documents' -UserData
+    ```
+
+    Use `-ApplicationData` for an application-data share. Use `-Performance` instead of `-Security` when the Performance profile's tradeoffs meet the workload requirements. This command creates only a share intent; it doesn't create a server intent.
+
+    When `Add-Intent` completes, SMB Policy Controller (preview) stores the desired share intent and attempts to apply it. The share intent retains the selected profile and settings if the server intent changes. To confirm the effective settings and client access, verify the intent.
+4. Immediately complete the verification procedure.
+
+---
+
+## Add a customized intent
+
+In SMB Policy Controller (preview), select the tab for the intent scope that you want to customize.
+
+# [Server-wide intent](#tab/server-wide-intent)
+For a new server-wide intent, use an override object when a supported setting must differ from the selected built-in profile. The following procedure creates a Security-profile server configuration, requires SMB server signing, and applies the customized object:
+
+1. Create and customize the override object.
+
+    ```powershell
+    $override = New-IntentOverride -Security
+    $override.SmbServerConfiguration.RequireSecuritySignature = $true
+    ```
+2. Add the customized server-wide intent.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Add-Intent -Override $override
+    ```
+
+    Don't combine `-Override` with `-Security` or `-Performance` on `Add-Intent`. The override object already contains the profile choice.
+3. Immediately complete the verification procedure.
+
+# [Share-level intent](#tab/share-level-intent)
+For a new share intent, use an override object when a supported setting must differ from the selected built-in profile. This procedure customizes one share intent; it doesn't create a named, reusable profile. The following procedure creates a Security-profile user-data configuration, requires encryption, and applies the customized object to the existing share:
+
+1. Create and customize the override object.
+
+    ```powershell
+    $override = New-IntentOverride -Security -UserData
+    $override.SmbShareConfiguration.EncryptData = $true
+    ```
+2. Add the customized share intent.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Add-Intent -ShareName 'Documents' -Override $override
+    ```
+
+    Don't combine `-Override` with `-Security`, `-Performance`, `-UserData`, or `-ApplicationData` on `Add-Intent`. The override object already contains those choices.
+
+    When `Add-Intent` completes, SMB Policy Controller (preview) stores the customized intent and starts an application attempt. To confirm the effective settings and client access, verify the intent.
+3. Immediately complete the verification procedure.
+
+---
+
+## Update an intent
+
+Use the get, edit, and set pattern to retain settings that you don't intend to change. A new override object uses a profile rather than cloning the existing intent or current live configuration. Select the tab for the intent scope that you want to update.
+
+# [Server-wide intent](#tab/server-wide-intent)
+1. Read the current server-wide intent.
+
+    ```powershell
+    $intent = Get-Intent -System
+    if ($null -eq $intent) {
+        throw "The server didn't return a readable server-wide intent."
+    }
+    $intent
+    ```
+2. Review the complete object and then change only the required property. This example requires SMB server signing.
+
+    ```powershell
+    $intent.SmbServerConfiguration.RequireSecuritySignature = $true
+    ```
+3. Submit the edited object.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Set-Intent -Override $intent
+    ```
+
+    When `Set-Intent` completes, SMB Policy Controller (preview) stores the updated intent and starts an application attempt. To confirm the effective settings and client access, verify the intent.
+4. Complete the verification procedure.
+
+# [Share-level intent](#tab/share-level-intent)
+To change selected retained settings, retrieve the existing share intent, edit only the required properties, and submit the edited intent with `Set-Intent`.
+
+1. Read the current share intent.
+
+    ```powershell
+    $intent = Get-Intent -ShareName 'Documents'
+    if ($null -eq $intent) {
+        throw "The cmdlet didn't return a readable share intent."
+    }
+    $intent
+    ```
+2. Review the complete object and change only the required property. This example requires encryption for the share.
+
+    ```powershell
+    $intent.SmbShareConfiguration.EncryptData = $true
+    ```
+3. Submit the edited object.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Set-Intent -ShareName 'Documents' -Override $intent
+    ```
+
+    When `Set-Intent` completes, SMB Policy Controller (preview) stores the updated share intent and starts an application attempt. To confirm the effective settings and client access, verify the intent.
+4. Complete the verification procedure.
+
+---
+
+These examples update selected settings within an existing intent type. They don't establish a profile migration procedure or a procedure for changing between user-data and application-data intent types.
+
+## Verify an intent
+
+Use three customer-facing evidence layers: the stored intent, the effective or observed configuration, and representative client success. Check each layer because a saved intent alone doesn't prove that the settings are effective or that clients can use the share. The installed Windows build can present different status details, so don't depend on specific field labels.
+
+1. Read the applicable stored intent to confirm the saved scope, profile, and settings.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Intent -System
+    Get-Intent -ShareName 'Documents'
+    ```
+
+    Run only the command for the scope you're verifying. Inspect the complete returned object and any available status information. Don't interpret a command error as proof that no intent exists.
+2. Read the effective or observed server and client configuration for a server-wide intent. This evidence shows whether the relevant host-wide settings match the stored intent.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-SmbServerConfiguration
+    Get-SmbClientConfiguration
+    ```
+3. Read the effective or observed share configuration for a share intent. This evidence shows whether the relevant share settings match the stored intent.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-SmbShare -Name 'Documents' -ErrorAction Stop |
+        Format-List Name, ScopeName, Path, Description, FolderEnumerationMode,
+            CachingMode, LeasingMode, CaTimeout, CompressData, ConcurrentUserLimit,
+            ContinuouslyAvailable, DirectoryHandleLeasing, DisableClientMetadataCaching,
+            EncryptData, IsolatedTransport
+    ```
+4. Compare every relevant managed setting with the stored intent and your approved change plan. Check each affected configuration group instead of relying on one summary result.
+5. For a server-wide intent, test representative outbound SMB client operations from the managed device against remote shares that it normally uses. If the managed device hosts shares, also test representative clients' inbound access. For a share intent, test the share from representative clients. Use representative user identities and workload operations, and verify the expected read, write, and denied-access cases that apply.
+6. Record the results and the observation time. Recheck after Group Policy, scripts, clustering operations, or other configuration tools change the same settings.
+
+## Retry intent application
+
+The system limits application retries. Retry only after you identify and correct the cause of the failure. Don't automate repeated retries or depend on an assumed retry schedule, attempt count, or counter-reset behavior.
+
+1. Confirm that the intent is active and that no operation is removing it.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Intent -System
+    Get-Intent -ShareName 'Documents'
+    ```
+
+    Run the command for the affected scope.
+2. Correct the underlying problem reported by SMB Policy Controller.
+
+    - Retry a server-wide intent.
+
+        ```powershell
+        Set-Intent -Retry
+        ```
+
+        For a share intent, run:
+
+        ```powershell
+        Set-Intent -ShareName 'Documents' -Retry
+        ```
+3. Complete the verification procedure.
+
+`Set-Intent -Retry` reapplies an active intent. It isn't a profile change, a rollback, or a retry of an incomplete removal. Don't place it in an uncontrolled loop.
+
+## Collect diagnostics
+
+Collect stored-intent, effective-state, service, and client evidence from the same time period. This information helps you distinguish controller problems from general SMB connectivity problems.
+
+1. Record the service and module state.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Service -Name PolicyController
+    Get-Module -ListAvailable -Name PolicyController
+    Get-Command -Module PolicyController
+    ```
+2. Capture the applicable intent object and any errors without changing it.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Intent -System
+    Get-Intent -ShareName 'Documents'
+    ```
+3. Capture the effective SMB settings.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-SmbServerConfiguration
+    Get-SmbClientConfiguration
+    Get-SmbShare -Name 'Documents' -ErrorAction Stop |
+        Format-List Name, ScopeName, Path, Description, FolderEnumerationMode,
+            CachingMode, LeasingMode, CaTimeout, CompressData, ConcurrentUserLimit,
+            ContinuouslyAvailable, DirectoryHandleLeasing, DisableClientMetadataCaching,
+            EncryptData, IsolatedTransport
+    ```
+4. Record the server time, affected share identity, client identity, operation, and error message. Include any observation time that the intent reports.
+5. Review the SMB client and server event logs for the same period. For log locations and general connectivity checks, see [Troubleshoot SMB](troubleshoot/troubleshooting-smb).
+6. If your support process requires controller-specific tracing, first inspect the tracing help that the installed module supplies.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Help Set-IntentTracing -Full
+    ```
+
+    Follow only the trace procedure, output location, and data-handling requirements in the help for the installed PolicyController module. This article doesn't assume a trace path, provider, file size, or remote-tracing behavior.
+
+## Remove an intent and return to previous settings
+
+Select the tab for the intent scope that you want to remove.
+
+# [Server-wide intent](#tab/server-wide-intent)
+When removal succeeds, SMB Policy Controller (preview) returns managed host settings to the values that it captured before it first applied the intent, not to Security or Performance profile defaults. Removing a server-wide intent affects the managed SMB server, SMB client, registry, and alternative-port configuration. Account for every server and share target that broad removal selects before continuing.
+
+1. Record the server-wide intent and all relevant effective server settings.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Intent -System
+    Get-SmbServerConfiguration
+    Get-SmbClientConfiguration
+    ```
+2. Use your change plan and intent records to account for every persisted or incomplete share-intent lifetime that broad removal can select. For every affected share that still exists, record its stored intent and relevant effective managed settings. Replace `Documents` with the share name, and repeat these commands for every affected existing share. If you can't account for every target and its baseline, don't use broad removal.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Intent -ShareName 'Documents'
+    Get-SmbShare -Name 'Documents' -ErrorAction Stop |
+        Format-List Name, ScopeName, Path, Description, FolderEnumerationMode,
+            CachingMode, LeasingMode, CaTimeout, CompressData, ConcurrentUserLimit,
+            ContinuouslyAvailable, DirectoryHandleLeasing, DisableClientMetadataCaching,
+            EncryptData, IsolatedTransport
+    ```
+3. Review the installed module help and your change plan before you use broad removal.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Help Remove-Intent -Full
+    ```
+4. Start the server-wide removal.
+
+    Warning
+
+    Running `Remove-Intent` without parameters is equivalent to `Remove-Intent -System`. It selects the server intent and all persisted or incomplete share-intent lifetimes, and it doesn't prompt for confirmation. The operation can partially complete or fail. In a cluster, resource ownership or offline participating nodes can delay completion or cause it to fail. You must specify `-ShareName` for share-only removal.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Remove-Intent -System
+    ```
+
+    During successful processing, SMB Policy Controller returns the managed settings that it captured to their pre-intent values before it finishes removing each intent that the operation selected.
+5. Verify that the removal completed for every target that the operation selected and that SMB Policy Controller returned the managed settings to their pre-intent values. Check the effective configuration instead of assuming that command submission means that the operation completed.
+6. Compare effective settings with the pre-intent records for each affected target, and test representative client access.
+7. If removal doesn't complete, preserve the evidence and correct the reported cause.
+8. After you correct the reported cause, run `Remove-Intent -System` to retry any incomplete removals. Don't use `Set-Intent -Retry`, which retries application of an active intent, and don't manually delete controller recovery records.
+
+The removal operation doesn't delete shares or data, and it isn't a backup restore. SMB Policy Controller returns the managed settings that it captured to their pre-intent values.
+
+# [Share-level intent](#tab/share-level-intent)
+When removal succeeds, SMB Policy Controller (preview) returns the managed share settings to the values that it captured before it first applied the intent, not to Security or Performance profile defaults. Removing a share intent can affect live client access, so use an explicit scope and verify the effective settings and client operations afterward.
+
+1. Record the stored intent, effective share settings, share name, scope, and path.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Intent -ShareName 'Documents'
+    Get-SmbShare -Name 'Documents' -ErrorAction Stop |
+        Format-List Name, ScopeName, Path, Description, FolderEnumerationMode,
+            CachingMode, LeasingMode, CaTimeout, CompressData, ConcurrentUserLimit,
+            ContinuouslyAvailable, DirectoryHandleLeasing, DisableClientMetadataCaching,
+            EncryptData, IsolatedTransport
+    ```
+2. Remove the named share intent.
+
+    ```powershell
+    Remove-Intent -ShareName 'Documents'
+    ```
+3. Verify that removal completed and returned the managed settings to their pre-intent values. Don't treat command submission alone as proof of success.
+4. Compare the effective managed share settings with the pre-intent record, and test representative client access.
+5. If removal doesn't complete, preserve the evidence and correct the reported cause.
+6. After you correct the reported cause, run the same `Remove-Intent -ShareName 'Documents'` command to retry the incomplete removal. Don't use `Set-Intent -Retry`, which retries application of an active intent rather than removal.
+
+The removal operation doesn't delete the share or its files, and it isn't a backup restore. It returns the managed settings to the values that SMB Policy Controller captured before it applied the intent.
+
+---
+
+## Troubleshoot common problems
+
+Use the following guidance after collecting diagnostics. Don't delete controller recovery records or apply undocumented repair commands.
+
+| Problem | Recommended action |
+| --- | --- |
+| Add reports that an intent already exists | Read the existing intent, then use the get, edit, and set pattern. Don't remove it only to make Add succeed. |
+| The system can't find the share | Confirm its exact name, path, and scope with `Get-SmbShare`. SMB Policy Controller (preview) doesn't create the share. |
+| Stored intent and effective settings differ | Check reported application errors, service health, setting applicability, ownership, and other configuration writers. Inspect every managed group because application might be partial. |
+| Drift returns after correction | Check for Group Policy, scripts, management tools, or administrators that write the same settings. Coordinate writers instead of repeatedly forcing changes. |
+| Client access fails although settings appear compliant | Troubleshoot authentication, authorization, networking, name resolution, dialect negotiation, and the client workload separately. A compliance observation isn't a client-access test. |
+| Retry doesn't resolve the problem | Stop retrying, preserve the evidence, and investigate the underlying error. |
+| Removal doesn't complete | Preserve the evidence, correct the reported cause, and retry the same `Remove-Intent` command. |

+# SMB Policy Controller (preview) overview in Windows Server | Microsoft Learn
+
+SMB Policy Controller (preview) stores an administrator-defined Server Message Block (SMB) configuration and keeps managed settings aligned with it. Use SMB Policy Controller to maintain a consistent SMB configuration for a server or an existing share. An *intent* is a saved configuration that specifies the SMB settings for a server or share. The controller stores the configuration, applies the managed settings, and attempts to correct any settings that drift.
+
+This article explains server and share intent scopes, profiles, and workload selectors. It also explains how the controller reconciles settings and restores captured settings after you remove an intent. Use this information to decide whether and how to use SMB Policy Controller.
+
+Important
+
+SMB Policy Controller is currently in PREVIEW. This information relates to a prerelease product that may be substantially modified before it's released. Microsoft makes no warranties, expressed or implied, with respect to the information provided here.
+
+## Server and share intent
+
+SMB Policy Controller (preview) uses complementary server and share intent scopes. A server intent manages host-wide settings, while a share intent manages one existing named share.
+
+| Intent | What it manages | What to consider |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Server intent | Host-wide SMB server configuration, SMB client configuration, and related host settings, including managed registry and alternative-port configuration | Changes affect multiple shares, inbound client access, and outbound SMB connections from the host. |
+| Share intent | The effective configuration of one existing named SMB share | Create the share first. Its path, permissions, storage, and availability design remain separate. |
+
+SMB Policy Controller manages SMB settings as part of a wider file-service solution. It doesn't create shares, configure storage, grant access, manage firewall rules, or provide backups. Workload compatibility, security architecture, storage, and availability remain separate design decisions.
+
+For example, you can use the Security profile for the server and the Performance profile for a workload-specific share. Server and share profiles are independent. If you create a share intent without selecting a profile, it inherits the profile selected by the stored server intent. If the stored server intent is missing or the controller can't read it, explicitly select Security or Performance; otherwise, the controller can't create the share intent. After creation, the share retains its profile and settings when the server intent changes. Because server and share intents have separate scopes, verify their combined effective settings.
+
+When you add or update an intent, the controller stores the desired configuration and attempts to apply it. It then compares managed SMB settings with the stored intent and reapplies settings that differ. Storing and applying are separate outcomes: one setting group can apply successfully while another fails.
+
+SMB Policy Controller doesn't have universal precedence over Group Policy, scripts, administrators, or other configuration tools. Coordinate systems that change the same settings to avoid repeated drift. To compare stored intent, effective settings, and representative client access, see [Verify an intent](configure-smb-policy-controller#verify-an-intent).
+
+## Profiles and workload selectors
+
+SMB Policy Controller (preview) provides two built-in profile choices: Security and Performance:
+
+- **Security** selects settings that strengthen SMB protection.
+- **Performance** selects settings that favor workload performance.
+
+For a server intent, a profile supplies SMB server, SMB client, and managed registry settings. For a share intent, a profile supplies SMB share settings. The following tabs present all 106 profile settings and implemented override properties.
+
+The profile tables explicitly configure Boolean values rather than leaving them unset or inferring them. For SMB server and client properties, the controller passes these values to `Set-SmbServerConfiguration` or `Set-SmbClientConfiguration`. The tables list the Boolean values that `Get-SmbServerConfiguration` and `Get-SmbClientConfiguration` return.
+
+The tables distinguish configured values from their runtime interpretation. Validate runtime behavior, tuning suitability, and build compatibility for your workload before deployment.
+
+For general protocol details, see [Server Message Block (SMB) Protocol Versions 2 and 3 specification](/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-smb2/5606ad47-5ee0-437a-817e-70c366052962).
+
+Profile names don't guarantee regulatory compliance, workload compatibility, a specific throughput level, or protection against every threat. Inspect the complete profile-derived object and assess its effect on clients before you apply it. For related guidance, see [SMB security hardening](smb-security-hardening) and [SMB over QUIC](smb-over-quic).
+
+# [SMB server](#tab/smb-server)
+The SMB server profiles define 56 settings. Settings with different Security and Performance values appear first.
+
+### Profile differences
+
+| SMB server setting | Security value | Performance value |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `AuditClientCertificateAccess` | True | False |
+| `AuditClientDoesNotSupportEncryption` | True | False |
+| `AuditClientDoesNotSupportSigning` | True | False |
+| `AuditInsecureGuestLogon` | True | False |
+| `AuditSmb1Access` | True | False |
+| `DisableCompression` | True | False |
+| `EnableAuthRateLimiter` | True | False |
+| `EnableDirectoryHandleLeasing` | False | True |
+| `EnableLeasing` | False | True |
+| `EnableSecuritySignature` | True | False |
+| `EnableSMBQUIC` | False | True |
+| `EncryptData` | True | False |
+| `EncryptionCiphers` | `AES_256_GCM`, `AES_256_CCM` | `AES_128_GCM`, `AES_128_CCM`, `AES_256_GCM`, `AES_256_CCM` |
+| `RejectUnencryptedAccess` | True | False |
+| `RequestCompression` | False | True |
+| `RequireSecuritySignature` | True | False |
+| `RestrictNamedpipeAccessViaQuic` | True | False |
+| `TreatHostAsStableStorage` | False | True |
+
+### Common settings
+
+| SMB server setting | Security and Performance value |
+| --- | --- |
+| `AsynchronousCredits` | Maximum configured value (4,294,967,295) |
+| `AutoDisconnectTimeoutInMinutesV1` | Disabled |
+| `AutoDisconnectTimeoutInSecondsV2` | 900 seconds |
+| `AutoShareServer` | False |
+| `AutoShareWorkstation` | False |
+| `DisableSmbEncryptionOnSecureConnection` | False |
+| `DurableHandleV2TimeoutInSeconds` | 180 |
+| `EnableAuthenticateUserSharing` | False |
+| `EnableDownlevelTimewarp` | False |
+| `EnableForcedLogoff` | True |
+| `EnableMailslots` | False |
+| `EnableMultiChannel` | True |
+| `EnableOplocks` | False |
+| `EnableSMB1Protocol` | False |
+| `EnableSMB2Protocol` | True |
+| `EnableStrictNameChecking` | False |
+| `InvalidAuthenticationDelayTimeInMs` | 2,000 |
+| `IrpStackSize` | 15 |
+| `KeepAliveTime` | 2 |
+| `MaxChannelPerSession` | 32 |
+| `MaxMpxCount` | 50 |
+| `MaxSessionPerConnection` | 16,384 |
+| `MaxThreadsPerQueue` | 20 |
+| `MaxWorkItems` | 1 |
+| `NullSessionPipes` | Profile-managed list; validate the effective contents |
+| `NullSessionShares` | Profile-managed list; validate the effective contents |
+| `OplockBreakWait` | 35 |
+| `PendingClientTimeoutInSeconds` | 120 |
+| `ServerHidden` | True |
+| `Smb2CreditsMax` | 2,048 |
+| `Smb2CreditsMin` | 128 |
+| `Smb2DialectMax` | `SMB311` |
+| `Smb2DialectMin` | `SMB311` |
+| `SmbServerNameHardeningLevel` | 2 |
+| `ValidateAliasNotCircular` | True |
+| `ValidateShareScope` | True |
+| `ValidateShareScopeNotAliased` | True |
+| `ValidateTargetName` | True |
+
+On some downlevel systems, the SMB server runtime adjusts `MaxWorkItems` upward to a processor-count multiple. The SMB server ignores `Smb2CreditsMin` on Windows 10 and later and on Windows Server 2016 and later. The SMB server no longer uses `MaxThreadsPerQueue`.
+
+Before you apply a profile, review the effective `NullSessionPipes` and `NullSessionShares` lists and assess the resulting anonymous-session access.
+
+# [SMB client](#tab/smb-client)
+The SMB client profiles define 33 settings. Settings with different Security and Performance values appear first.
+
+### Profile differences
+
+| SMB client setting | Security value | Performance value |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `AuditInsecureGuestLogon` | True | False |
+| `AuditServerDoesNotSupportEncryption` | True | False |
+| `AuditServerDoesNotSupportSigning` | True | False |
+| `BlockNTLM` | True | False |
+| `DisableCompression` | True | False |
+| `EnableLargeMtu` | False | True |
+| `EnableSecuritySignature` | True | False |
+| `EnableSMBQUIC` | False | True |
+| `EncryptionCiphers` | `AES_256_GCM`, `AES_256_CCM` | `AES_128_GCM`, `AES_128_CCM`, `AES_256_GCM`, `AES_256_CCM` |
+| `SkipCertificateCheck` | False | True |
+| `RequestCompression` | False | True |
+| `RequireEncryption` | True | False |
+| `RequireSecuritySignature` | True | False |
+| `MaxCmds` | 50 | 32 |
+| `MaximumConnectionCountPerServer` | 50 | 32 |
+
+For an SMB over QUIC client, the Performance value `SkipCertificateCheck=True` removes the requirement for the server certificate to chain to a trusted issuer, which can allow connections that use a self-signed certificate. This value is a security tradeoff. It doesn't disable Transport Layer Security (TLS) encryption or all certificate processing.
+
+### Common settings
+
+| SMB client setting | Security and performance value |
+| --- | --- |
+| `BlockNTLMServerExceptionList` | Empty list |
+| `CompressibilitySamplingSize` | Maximum allowable (8 PiB) |
+| `CompressibleThreshold` | Maximum allowable (8 PiB) |
+| `EnableCompressibilitySampling` | False |
+| `ConnectionCountPerRssNetworkInterface` | 4 |
+| `DormantFileLimit` | 1,023 |
+| `EnableBandwidthThrottling` | False |
+| `EnableByteRangeLockingOnReadOnlyFiles` | False |
+| `EnableInsecureGuestLogons` | False |
+| `EnableMailslots` | False |
+| `EnableMultiChannel` | True |
+| `EnableLoadBalanceScaleOut` | False |
+| `DisabledSMBQUICServerExceptionList` | Empty list |
+| `ForceSMBEncryptionOverQuic` | False |
+| `UseOpportunisticLocking` | True |
+| `IgnoreRevocationOfflineErrors` | False |
+| `SMB2DialectMax` | `SMB311` |
+| `SMB2DialectMin` | `SMB311` |
+
+# [SMB share](#tab/smb-share)
+For a share intent, combine Security or Performance with one of two workload selectors:
+
+| Workload selector | Intended use | PowerShell identifier |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| User data | Shares that people and teams use interactively, such as shared document locations. | `-UserData` |
+| Application data | Shares that applications use for data rather than primarily for interactive document access. | `-ApplicationData` |
+
+User data and Application data are a closed two-value choice. They aren't additional profiles, and they affect only the 12 settings for the selected share. Within the Performance profile, the selector changes `CachingMode` from `Manual` for User data to `None` for Application data. Within the Security profile, it changes `FolderEnumerationMode` from `AccessBased` for User data to `Unrestricted` for Application data.
+
+If `Add-Intent` specifies only `-UserData` or `-ApplicationData`, the share intent inherits the profile that the stored server intent selects. If that server intent is missing or unreadable, you can't create the share intent. Explicitly select Security or Performance to avoid this dependency. After creation, the share retains its profile and settings when the server intent changes.
+
+| SMB share setting | Performance and User data | Performance and Application data | Security and User data | Security and Application data |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| `FolderEnumerationMode` | `Unrestricted` | `Unrestricted` | `AccessBased` | `Unrestricted` |
+| `CachingMode` | `Manual` | `None` | `None` | `None` |
+| `LeasingMode` | `Full` | `Full` | `Full` | `Full` |
+| `CaTimeout` | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
+| `CompressData` | True | True | False | False |
+| `ConcurrentUserLimit` | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
+| `ContinuouslyAvailable` | True | True | False | False |
+| `DirectoryHandleLeasing` | True | True | False | False |
+| `DisableClientMetadataCaching` | False | False | True | True |
+| `EncryptData` | False | False | True | True |
+| `IsolatedTransport` | False | False | True | True |
+| `Description` | Share intent configured by Policy manager | Share intent configured by Policy manager | Share intent configured by Policy manager | Share intent configured by Policy manager |
+
+The `ContinuouslyAvailable=True` Performance value applies to both workload selectors. It requests continuous availability but doesn't create a cluster, configure suitable storage, or guarantee availability. For configuration procedures, use the **Share-level intent** tab in [Configure an intent](configure-smb-policy-controller#configure-an-intent).
+
+# [Host settings](#tab/host-settings)
+A server profile also defines these three managed registry settings:
+
+| Host registry setting | Security value | Performance value |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `AdditionalCriticalWorkerThreads` | `Environment.ProcessorCount` | `2 * Environment.ProcessorCount` |
+| `MaxThreadsPerNumaNode` | 20 | 20 |
+| `RemoteFileDirtyPageThreshold` | 1,310,720 | 2,621,440 |
+
+The system implements `TransportType` and `Port` as alternative-port override properties, but Security and Performance profiles supply no alternative-port entries. The initial alternative-port collection is empty.
+
+| Override property | Type | Initial profile value |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `TransportType` | Nullable transport type | No entry |
+| `Port` | Nullable unsigned 16-bit integer | No entry |
+
+---
+
+## Profile-derived overrides
+
+In SMB Policy Controller (preview), an *override object* is an editable PowerShell configuration object for one intent. `New-IntentOverride` creates a new, complete object from the selected built-in profile. It isn't a sparse patch, a copy of the current effective configuration, or a copy of an existing intent.
+
+One override object can contain multiple modified settings. Creating the object doesn't store or apply it. When you add the intent, the controller processes the complete object. Server setting groups use separate providers, so groups can apply or fail independently rather than as one transaction.
+
+To update an existing intent while retaining its other choices, retrieve the existing intent object, edit the required settings, and submit that object with `Set-Intent`. Don't use a new profile-derived object as a copy of the existing intent. For the procedures, use the **Share-level intent** tab in [Add a customized intent](configure-smb-policy-controller#add-a-customized-intent) and see [Update an intent](configure-smb-policy-controller#update-an-intent).
+
+## How does SMB Policy Controller (preview) reconcile intents in a Windows Server failover cluster?
+
+In a Windows Server failover cluster, nodes share the desired server intent, but each node reconciles that intent against its own local SMB configuration. Nodes can converge at different times, especially when a node is offline or encounters an error.
+
+The current owner of the clustered resource that owns the share reconciles a share intent. Ownership changes, unavailable owners, and offline nodes can delay convergence or cause reconciliation to fail.
+
+SMB Policy Controller (preview) doesn't design or create the cluster. A shared intent doesn't promise simultaneous effective settings across nodes, uninterrupted availability, or that a workload and storage configuration supports every requested setting.
+
+## What happens to captured settings when you remove an SMB Policy Controller (preview) intent?
+
+Before SMB Policy Controller (preview) first applies an intent, it captures the existing values of the settings that the intent manages. The intent retains those values throughout its life. Updating, reapplying, or retrying the intent doesn't replace them.
+
+When `Remove-Intent` completes successfully, the controller returns the managed settings to the captured pre-policy values and verifies the effective values. It doesn't return settings to profile defaults or to a previous intent revision, and it isn't a backup restore operation. Removing a share intent doesn't delete the share or its data.
+
+Caution
+
+Restoring captured pre-policy values can re-enable weaker SMB settings. After removal, review the resulting effective settings and confirm that they meet your current security requirements.
+
+Starting removal doesn't prove that restoration completed. An unavailable cluster node or share owner can delay completion, and one target can fail after another target succeeds. Verify the effective managed settings and client access after removal. For the scoped procedures, select the **Share-level intent** or **Server-wide intent** tab in [Remove an intent and return to previous settings](configure-smb-policy-controller#remove-an-intent-and-return-to-previous-settings).

-# Install Network HUD for Windows Server (preview) | Microsoft Learn
+# Install Network HUD on Windows Server clusters | Microsoft Learn
 
-Important
+Network HUD is a host networking diagnostics tool that identifies configuration and operational conditions in physical Windows Server clusters. It helps cluster administrators investigate network reliability issues by correlating host and physical network information that they otherwise need to gather separately.
 
-Network HUD for Windows Server is currently in PREVIEW. This information relates to a prerelease product that might be substantially modified before it's released. Microsoft makes no warranties, expressed or implied, with respect to the information provided here.
+In this article, you install Network HUD on each Azure Arc-enabled machine in a Windows Server 2025 Datacenter cluster, verify detection initialization, and view active cluster health faults.
 
-Network HUD is a cluster‑aware, intent‑driven host networking diagnostics tool that continuously analyzes adapters, links, and switch signals to surface actionable health faults early. This article explains how to enable Network HUD on an Azure Arc connected Windows Server 2025 Datacenter clustered deployment and how to view health faults using Windows Admin Center or PowerShell.
+## Prerequisites for installing Network HUD
 
-## Prerequisites
+- A failover cluster with at least two physical machines that meet the [Storage Spaces Direct hardware requirements](../storage/storage-spaces/storage-spaces-direct-hardware-requirements). Network HUD doesn't support installation on virtual machines.
+- Windows Server 2025 Datacenter installed on each cluster node.
+- Hyper-V role and management tools installed on each cluster node.
+- Network ATC configured with host networking intents. For more information, see [Network ATC overview](/en-us/azure/azure-local/concepts/network-atc-overview?pivots=windows-server).
+- Storage Spaces Direct enabled. For more information, see [Deploy Storage Spaces Direct on Windows Server](../storage/storage-spaces/deploy-storage-spaces-direct).
+- Data Center Bridging and Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP) tools installed on each cluster node.
+- Each cluster node connected to Azure Arc and enrolled in Windows Server Management enabled by Azure Arc. For more information, see [Windows Server Management enabled by Azure Arc](/en-us/azure/azure-arc/servers/windows-server-management-overview). Network HUD doesn't support offline installation.
+- Validated physical switches that meet the applicable **Network switches for Azure Local** and **Network switch requirements** in [Physical network requirements for Azure Local](/en-us/azure/azure-local/concepts/physical-network-requirements).
+- Connected physical switch ports that advertise the LLDP information required for the cluster nodes' traffic roles. Network HUD uses these advertisements for physical-network checks.
+- The Azure Connected Machine Resource Administrator role, Contributor role, or a custom role with equivalent permissions on each Azure Arc-enabled server resource.
+- Administrative access to the cluster nodes for local PowerShell checks.
+- Access to a Windows Admin Center instance that can manage the cluster for the Windows Admin Center procedure.
 
-Before you install Network HUD, ensure you have the following prerequisites in place:
+## Install Network HUD on each cluster node
 
-- Windows Server Failover Clustering requirements:
+The Azure Arc extension installs the Network HUD service and PowerShell module. It doesn't configure the prerequisites.
 
-    - You have at least one node in the cluster.
-    - Cluster nodes must be running Windows Server 2025 Datacenter.
-    - Network ATC is deployed with host networking intents. To learn more about deploying Network ATC, see [Deploy host networking with Network ATC](/en-us/azure/azure-local/concepts/network-atc-overview?pivots=windows-server).
-    - The cluster must have Storage Spaces Direct (S2D) enabled. To learn more about deploying Storage Spaces Direct, see [Deploy Storage Spaces Direct on Windows Server](../storage/storage-spaces/deploy-storage-spaces-direct).
-    - Each cluster node has the `DataCenterBridging LLDP Tools` installed from the Remote Server Administration Tools feature.
-- Azure Arc requirements:
+1. In the [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com), search for and select **Machines - Azure Arc**.
+2. Select a cluster node.
+3. On the node's **Overview** page, under **Capabilities**, select the **Network HUD** tile.
 
-    - Each cluster node must be connected to Azure Arc.
-    - You must be eligible for Windows Server Management enabled by Azure Arc. To learn more about the availability of the Network HUD benefit, see [Windows Server Management enabled by Azure Arc](/en-us/azure/azure-arc/servers/windows-server-management-overview).
-    - Network HUD is only available on machines in the following regions:
-        - East US 2 EUAP
-        - Central US EUAP
-        - Central US
-        - East US 2
-        - East US
-        - Canada Central
-        - West US 2
-        - North Europe
-        - West Europe
-        - Japan East
-        - Southeast Asia
-        - Australia East
-- Network HUD for Windows Server has the same network switch requirements as Azure Local. When using Network HUD on Windows Server, ensure you're using validated physical switches for Azure Local and that the network switch requirements are met. To learn more, review the sections ***Network switches for Azure Local*** and ***Network switch requirements*** in [Physical network requirements for Azure Local](/en-us/azure/azure-local/concepts/physical-network-requirements). Other sections in the Physical network requirements for Azure Local article don't apply to Network HUD Windows. Server
+    [![Screenshot of an Azure Arc-enabled server Overview page in the Azure portal, with Capabilities selected and Network HUD marked Not Configured.](media/install-network-hud/network-hud-azure-arc.png)](media/install-network-hud/network-hud-azure-arc.png#lightbox)
+4. Select **Enable**.
+5. Wait until the Azure Arc extension operation succeeds and the **Network HUD** tile reports **Enabled**.
+6. Repeat these steps for every cluster node. Install the extension on each Azure Arc-enabled machine, rather than once per cluster.
 
-## Enable the Network HUD extension in the Azure portal
+## Verify Network HUD extension deployment
 
-To use the Azure portal to enable the Network HUD extension, follow these steps:
+In the Azure portal, verify the extension deployment on every cluster node.
 
-1. Navigate to the [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com), then search for and select **Machines - Azure Arc**.
-2. Select the machine you want to enable the Network HUD extension on.
-3. Select the **Network HUD** tile.
+1. Open each node's Azure Arc resource.
+2. Under **Settings**, select **Extensions**, and then inspect the Network HUD extension deployment status.
+3. If a deployment failed, review its error details before retrying the deployment.
 
-    ![Screenshot of the Azure portal Machines - Azure Arc page showing the Network HUD extension tile before it's enabled.](media/install-network-hud/network-hud-azure-arc.png)
-4. When ready, select **Enable**.
-5. Once the extension is successfully enabled, you see a confirmation message and the tile shows as **Enabled**.
+## Verify Network HUD initialization
 
-## View health faults
+Perform these checks locally on every cluster node.
 
-To verify installation and view health faults, select your preferred method.
+1. Open PowerShell as an administrator.
+2. Verify that the `NetworkHUD` service is running:
 
-# [Windows Admin Center](#tab/windowsadmincenter)
-To verify the installation and view health faults using Windows Admin Center, follow these steps:
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Service -Name NetworkHUD
+    ```
+3. Verify that the Network HUD PowerShell module is available:
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-Module -ListAvailable -Name Az.StackHCI.NetworkHUD
+    ```
+4. Use `Get-WinEvent` to query events 105, 106, and 111 in the `Microsoft-Windows-Networking-NetworkHUD/Operational` log since the current service start time:
+
+    ```powershell
+    $service = Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Service -Filter "Name = 'NetworkHUD'"
+    $serviceStartTime = (Get-Process -Id $service.ProcessId).StartTime
+    
+    Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
+        LogName      = 'Microsoft-Windows-Networking-NetworkHUD/Operational'
+        ProviderName = 'Microsoft-Windows-Networking-NetworkHUD'
+        Id           = 105, 106, 111
+        StartTime    = $serviceStartTime
+    } -MaxEvents 20 |
+        Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, LevelDisplayName, Message
+    ```
+5. Verify that the current service startup has event 105, which confirms initialization, and event 111, which confirms that Network HUD loaded scenarios. Event 106 reports an initialization failure.
+
+A running service confirms only that the service started. It doesn't confirm that Network HUD detections initialized.
+
+## View active Network HUD health faults
+
+After you confirm initialization, view active health faults by using Windows Admin Center or PowerShell.
 
+# [Windows Admin Center](#tab/windowsadmincenter)
 1. Open Windows Admin Center and connect to your Windows Server 2025 Datacenter cluster.
-2. In the Cluster view, either view alerts from the dashboard or select the notification bell icon on the top right corner.
+2. In the cluster view, view alerts on the dashboard or select the notification bell icon.
 
-    ![Screenshot of Windows Admin Center cluster dashboard displaying active alerts including a Network HUD networking fault.](media/install-network-hud/windows-admin-center-alerts.png)
-3. Look for alerts related to Network HUD. These alerts provide information about any detected host networking issues.
-4. Select an alert to view more details and recommended actions for remediation.
+    [![Windows Admin Center cluster dashboard displaying active alerts, including a Network HUD networking fault.](media/network-hud/windows-admin-center-alerts.png)](media/network-hud/windows-admin-center-alerts.png#lightbox)
+3. Look for Network HUD alerts.
+4. Select an alert to view its details and recommended actions.
 
-    ![Screenshot of Windows Admin Center fault detail pane for a Network HUD alert showing fields and recommended remediation actions.](media/install-network-hud/windows-admin-center-alert-detail.png)
+    ![Windows Admin Center fault detail pane for a Network HUD alert showing fields and recommended remediation actions.](media/install-network-hud/windows-admin-center-alert-detail.png)
 
-Alerts automatically resolve themselves when the underlying issue is fixed.
+Network HUD clears an alert after it no longer detects the underlying condition.
 
-# [PowerShell](#tab/powershell)
-To verify the installation and view health faults using PowerShell, follow these steps:
+Clearing an alert doesn't mean that Network HUD automatically repaired the underlying issue.
 
-1. Sign in to your administrative machine with an account that has the necessary permissions to access the Windows Server 2025 Datacenter cluster.
-2. Open PowerShell and import the FailoverClusters module:
+# [PowerShell](#tab/powershell)
+1. Open PowerShell as an administrator on a cluster node.
+2. Import the Failover Clusters module:
 
     ```powershell
     Import-Module FailoverClusters
     ```
-3. Get the cluster object to connect to your cluster, replacing `<YourClusterName>` with the name of your cluster:
+3. Get active cluster health faults for Network HUD:
 
     ```powershell
-    $cluster = Get-Cluster -Name "<YourClusterName>"
+    Get-HealthFault | Where-Object Reason -like '*HUD*'
     ```
-4. To get health faults related to Network HUD, run the following command:
+
+Run the command once on any cluster node. An empty result means that the query returned no active Network HUD health faults. It doesn't confirm that Network HUD detections initialized.
+
+---
+
+## Troubleshoot Network HUD installation and initialization failures
+
+Troubleshoot locally on the affected node.
+
+1. If you can't enable Network HUD, review extension errors in the Azure portal and logs on the affected node.
+2. Verify that the required Windows features are installed, Network ATC intents are configured, Storage Spaces Direct is enabled, the node is connected to Azure Arc, and Windows Server Management enabled by Azure Arc enrollment is active.
+3. Import the Network HUD PowerShell module:
 
     ```powershell
-    Get-HealthFault -Cluster $cluster | Where Reason -like '*hud*'
+    Import-Module Az.StackHCI.NetworkHUD
     ```
-5. The command output displays a list of Network HUD related health faults, including details about the issue and a recommended resolution. The following is an example output:
+4. Review recent Network HUD Operational events for service initialization and scenario loading:
 
     ```powershell
-    FaultId      : 1015
-    
-    Reason       : Network HUD detected incorrect VLAN configuration
-    
-    Severity     : Warning
-    
-    NodeName     : ClusterNode01
-    
-    Timestamp    : 11/04/2025 09:15:32
-    
-    Resolution   : Verify VLAN settings on NIC and switch ports
+    Get-NetHUDLog -OperationalLog
     ```
+5. Review recent Network HUD Diagnostic events for scenario results:
+
+    ```powershell
+    Get-NetHUDLog -ContentLog
+    ```
+
+    Diagnostic event 102 reports scenario success, and event 103 reports scenario failure. These diagnostic events aren't cluster health faults.
+6. If you can't import the `Az.StackHCI.NetworkHUD` module, investigate the extension deployment status and Azure Arc extension logs.
+7. If the extension deployment failed, follow [Troubleshoot Azure Arc-enabled servers VM extension issues](/en-us/azure/azure-arc/servers/troubleshoot-vm-extensions).
 
----
\ No newline at end of file
+Don't treat a running service, an empty health-fault query, or missing log output as evidence that initialization succeeded. Review Operational events 105, 106, and 111 to determine initialization status.

-Important
+Network HUD is a host networking diagnostics tool for physical Windows Server 2025 Datacenter failover clusters. It uses Network ATC intent data and signals from cluster nodes, network adapters, and physical switches to detect configuration and operational conditions and report them as cluster health faults.
 
-Network HUD for Windows Server is currently in PREVIEW. This information relates to a prerelease product that may be substantially modified before it's released. Microsoft makes no warranties, expressed or implied, with respect to the information provided here.
+Network HUD helps cluster administrators correlate host and physical network information without gathering it separately. Its detections identify conditions for administrators to investigate; Network HUD doesn't automatically remediate the reported conditions or guarantee that workloads avoid performance or connectivity problems.
 
-Network HUD is a host networking diagnostics and operational tool that analyzes and remediates host networking issues. Network HID runs continuously, correlating physical switch links, host adapter settings, and the cluster roles that consume them. Using network intent data, Network HUD selects relevant tests and raises early alerts when emerging issues threaten workload performance or stability.
+Network HUD helps you:
 
-Host networking can be hard to troubleshoot because you need to gather information from the physical fabric switches, cluster hosts, network adapters settings, and guest workloads. This separation obscures root causes, slows remediation, and increases the risk of performance or stability degradation. Network HUD helps you to:
+- Identify physical network misconfigurations, such as missing VLANs or Priority Flow Control (PFC) priorities.
+- Detect adapter instability and Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) bandwidth limitations.
+- Validate host networking configuration consistency and identify driver maintenance needs.
+- Review health faults and recommended actions in Windows Admin Center or PowerShell.
 
-- Identify misconfiguration on the physical network. For example, missing VLAN or PFC priority.
-- Detect operational hardware issues, such as flapping or unstable adapters, PCIe oversubscription.
-- Optimize and validate host configuration symmetry and driver readiness.
-- Autoremediate selected conditions, such as removing persistently unstable adapters from service when safe to do so.
+After reading this article, you'll understand when Network HUD applies and how to use its detections and health faults to investigate host networking conditions.
 
-## Availability and requirements

-The following table defines some of the key terms used in this document:

 | Term | Definition |
 | --- | --- |
-| Network HUD: Network HUD | Windows Server Management enabled by Azure Arc benefit that analyzes and, where possible, remediates host networking issues. |
-| Network HUD: Content | Detection logic packages downloaded separately and updated over time; can run disconnected. |
-| Network HUD: Content Detection | Individual detection units that watch for behavior indicating an issue is occurring or likely to occur. |
-| Network ATC: Intent | Definition of how you intend to use one or more physical adapters. For example, a converged management/compute/storage set. Each physical adapter can belong to only one intent. |

+| Network HUD | A Windows Server Management enabled by Azure Arc benefit that detects host networking configuration and operational issues. |
+| Content | Logic that Network HUD uses to evaluate host and network signals. |

-Network HUD is cluster-aware and continuously interprets raw host and fabric signals in the context of declared Network ATC intents and cluster states. Instead of treating adapters, switches, and roles as isolated components, it correlates them across the cluster so you can understand emerging instability in an operational context. +Network HUD reports configuration and operational conditions through the cluster Health Service. The following table describes its detection inventory:
 
-| Detection | Purpose |
+| Network HUD detection | Condition detected |
 | --- | --- |
-| Failed Network ATC intents | Detects intents that don't provision completely (missing virtual adapters, QoS, storage settings) to prevent silent drift and unreliable baselines. |
-| Missing Network ATC intent types | Ensures required traffic roles (management, compute, storage) exist so role‑specific diagnostics run; absence reduces coverage and masks unmanaged traffic. |
-| PCIe bandwidth oversubscription | Compares aggregate NIC link rates to slot/PCIe lane capacity; oversubscription can cause throttling and inconsistent performance under load. |
-| Unstable (flapping) adapters | Flags frequent link resets or drops that trigger failovers, raise latency, and degrade throughput before workload impact escalates. |
-| Inbox (unsupported) production drivers | Identifies NICs that use only basic inbox drivers lacking advanced offloads and optimizations, increasing reliability and performance risk. |
-| Aging or out‑of‑date drivers | Assesses driver package age and surfaces early maintenance needs. Warns when a driver is more than one year old so you can plan an update. |
-| Driver version inconsistency | Detects mismatched versions across identical adapters, preventing asymmetric behavior, and unpredictable performance. |
-| LLDP operational status | Indicates LLDP packet absences or parsing failure, reducing physical switch link detection and degrading other fabric validation tests. |
-| Misconfigured or inconsistent VLANs | Compares advertised versus expected VLANs across the same-host intent members, the same intent across all hosts, and against the required workload (VM NIC) VLAN availability. Deviations risk VM connectivity loss or storage isolation failure. VLAN consistency across three discrete scopes to catch localized misconfiguration before it becomes a cluster issue: Same-host intent scope: Relevant switchports must advertise the same VLAN set to each adapter in the same Network ATC intent on a single host. Cluster intent scope: All switchports must advertise a consistent VLAN set to adapters in the same Network ATC intent across every host in the cluster. Workload availability scope: VLANs required for all compute workloads (VM NICs) must be advertised to each adapter participating in the same Network ATC intent on every host. |
-| Inconsistent Priority Flow Control (PFC) | For storage intent adapters, Network HUD compares LLDP-advertised priorities from the physical switch with host-configured PFC. Flags missing or mismatched settings can cause congestion, prolonged pause conditions, elevated latency, or storage (S2D) failures. Alignment of PFC priorities for RDMA storage traffic with host intent configuration. For storage intent adapters, PFC validation includes comparing the LLDP-advertised priorities from the switch with the priorities enabled by Network ATC on the host. Network HUD flags mismatched configurations to make sure congestion, prolonged pause conditions, elevated latency, or storage (S2D) failures don't occur. |
-

+| Failed Network ATC intents | Identifies intents that didn't provision completely, including missing virtual adapters, quality-of-service settings, or storage settings. |
+| Missing Network ATC intent types | Identifies missing traffic roles so administrators can determine whether the intended management, compute, storage, or stretch configuration is present. |
+| Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) bandwidth oversubscription | Compares aggregate network adapter link rates with the reported PCIe slot and lane capacity to identify potential oversubscription. |
+| Unstable (flapping) adapters | Identifies repeated adapter link-state changes or resets. |
+| Inbox drivers in production | Identifies adapters that use inbox drivers instead of validated vendor drivers. |
+| Aging drivers | Identifies drivers whose reported driver date is more than 12 months old by default. The detection doesn't use the driver installation date or determine whether a newer driver is available. |
+| Driver version inconsistency | Compares the major and minor driver versions that equivalent adapters report and identifies differences. |
+| LLDP operational status | Identifies missing LLDP packets or LLDP parsing failures that can limit physical switch and fabric validation. |
+| Misconfigured or inconsistent VLANs | Compares VLANs that switches advertise in three scopes: adapters in the same intent on one host, the same intent across cluster hosts, and VLAN availability for compute workload virtual machine (VM) network adapters on every adapter in that intent across the cluster. |
+| Inconsistent PFC | For storage intent adapters, compares the PFC priorities that the physical switch advertises through LLDP with the priorities that Network ATC enables on the host. |
